activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year, so there would be almost no seasons.
story:
The tide would come in by four o'clock, and Ms. Mansour had said the video had to be posted before then. Ivy set the flashlight on a folded towel, wedged it with two shells, and stood the beach ball globe Jagger had drawn continents on in the sand beside her.

"Okay, you hold the light," she said. "Lilly, you record. I'll delegate the talking to Jagger since he's the one who actually studied."

"I studied," Ivy said. "I just can't talk and spin at the same time." That part was true. The part she left out was that she still wasn't sure she understood the whole thing, which was a dilemma, since she was the one who had to write the script. Jagger's notes were three pages of arrows and circles and looked far too sophisticated for something that was supposed to take one minute to explain.

Jagger crouched by the beach ball and made it spin slowly. "Earth turns, sun stays put, boom."

"That's day and night," Lilly said from behind her phone. "We need seasons. Spin it tilted, like the real one."

Ivy tilted the ball, poking a stick through the top at an angle so it leaned like a sleepy fence post. She moved it around the flashlight in a slow circle. "Watch Florida," she said, tapping the smudge Jagger had drawn. As the ball traveled, Florida leaned toward the light, then away. "Summer, then winter. Same sun, same Earth. Only the lean changes."

"Now try it straight up," Lilly said. "I want a before-and-after shot."

Ivy pulled out the stick and held the ball perfectly upright, spinning it as she walked it around the flashlight. Florida caught the light the same way on every lap. Around and around, nothing changed. She stopped halfway through the third circle.

"What's wrong?" Jagger asked.

"Nothing's wrong. That's the problem. Look at it." She held the ball still. "If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year, so there would be almost no seasons. Florida would get the same light in June as in December."

Lilly lowered the phone. "So the tilt isn't a side detail. It's the whole thing."

"The whole thing," Ivy said. She grabbed the stick, pushed it back through the top of the ball, and tilted it over. "Start recording. Forty seconds to spare." Jagger clicked the flashlight on and off, off and on, and the little paper Florida swung from light into shadow and back.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
story:
Peyton was sprawled on the living room rug, halfway through her homework, when Sarina snatched her phone off the couch and started scrolling. "Sarina, give it back," Peyton said, but Sarina just laughed and kept reading the texts out loud, doing voices for each one, until she hit the message from Peyton's mom about the appointment with the counselor. Sarina's voice went flat. "You see someone for anxiety?"

Peyton's face burned. It was one thing to talk about stress with her mom, and another thing entirely to have it performed in her own living room like a scene in a play. She grabbed the phone and held it against her chest, and for a second neither of them said anything. Sarina looked embarrassed too, which was something, but she still shrugged and said, "It was just a joke. You're so sensitive lately."

After Sarina left, Peyton sat at the kitchen table and thought about what her counselor had said on Tuesday, that coping with big feelings works better when the people around you know the rules. The word she had written in her notebook was boundaries. A boundary was a limit you set about what you were comfortable with, like how people treated you, touched you, or used your stuff. Her phone was her stuff. Her messages were hers. The problem was that Sarina probably didn't even know a rule was being broken, because Peyton had never actually stated one out loud. She had only hinted, and hints, apparently, were not robust enough to survive Sarina's personality.

So Peyton tested it. She texted Sarina a single, plain sentence: "You can come over anytime, but you can't read my phone without asking first." Then she put the phone face down and finished her math homework, though she kept checking the corner of the table where it lay, her stomach tight every time it buzzed. That fluttering, waiting feeling was its own kind of stress, and she practiced the breathing trick from her session, in for four, out for four, until her hands stopped feeling cold.

The reply came before dinner. "Ok that's fair. Sorry about today. Also your hand hygiene is a crime, you had cheeto dust on the screen." Peyton laughed out loud, alone in the kitchen, and then typed back, "Bring snacks tomorrow and I'll consider forgiving you." She set the phone down and looked at it without dread for the first time all evening. Tomorrow, when Sarina walked in and reached for the remote instead of Peyton's phone, she would know whether the rule had stuck. She got two mugs down from the cupboard and left them on the counter for the morning.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes, but they always have the same number of protons.
story:
Rosalie spread her homework across her grandfather's kitchen table, which smelled faintly of coffee and pencil shavings. The assignment was due Monday, and it wanted something she could not yet do: find the number of protons in an element using the periodic table. Mr. Perera had shown the class a giant poster of it back at school, all those boxes with letters and tiny numbers, but Rosalie had been absent the day he explained what the numbers meant. Now she stared at the photocopy in front of her and felt like she was looking at a coded message.

Her grandfather had gone out to the garden, so she hunted through his bookshelves herself. Above them hung a model airplane he had built decades ago, its wooden propeller still slowly turning whenever the kitchen door let in a draft. She pulled down a fat science encyclopedia, but the periodic table inside was printed in a font so small it thwarted her completely; she could not even tell which number was which.

Then her phone buzzed. It was Farhan, from her science class. Did you figure out the proton thing? Wassim says he did it in five minutes.

Rosalie typed back, Not yet. I don't know which number to use.

Before Farhan could answer, the radio in the corner, which her grandfather always left on, caught her ear. A program about archaeology was describing a wooden boat dug out of a bog, thousands of years old. "The wood was dated using carbon-14," the presenter said. "Carbon-14 in the timber revealed when the tree was cut down."

Rosalie frowned. Carbon was carbon. She knew that much. But then why would anyone call it carbon-14, as if there were other carbons? Did heavier carbon have more protons? She traced the row of the photocopy with her finger until she found the C box. Two numbers sat there. A 12 above the C, and a 6 in the corner. She decided to test the simplest idea: if 6 meant protons, then the 12 must be something else, something that could change without the element changing.

She pulled out her notebook and wrote it out like a proof. Carbon has 6 protons. The 14 in carbon-14 is bigger than 12. If the protons stayed 6, then the extra had to come from somewhere else in the atom, and the only other particle in the middle was the neutron. So carbon-14 had 6 protons and more neutrons than ordinary carbon. It was still carbon, because it was the protons that made it so.

Farhan texted again. Wassim found a video. It says atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons.

Rosalie typed fast. Yes! And those versions are called isotopes. That's what carbon-14 is. But they always have the same number of protons, so carbon-14 is still carbon. She stared at the screen, hardly believing she had worked it out before the video told her. Her idea had held.

When her grandfather came back inside with muddy boots and a handful of tomatoes, she was already racing through the homework. Oxygen, 8 protons. Gold, 79 protons. Uranium, 92. Each box gave up its secret the moment she knew which number to read.

"Something good happened," her grandfather said.

"The number at the top of each box is the protons," Rosalie said, tapping the photocopy. "Six for carbon. Watch, I'll do iron." She set her pencil point below the Fe box and began, "Twenty-six protons, because..."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: An element's atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element.
story:
Muhammad spread his science notebook across the kitchen table and glared at the photocopied periodic table Mr. Brennan had handed out after class. Tomorrow there was a quiz, and Mr. Brennan had said, "You won't get numbers to memorize. You'll get an element and a question." That was the worst kind of quiz, in Muhammad's opinion, because he could not figure out what the question would even be.

Anderson arrived with his backpack and a bag of chips, dropped both on a chair, and leaned over the paper. "Which part are we supposed to know?"

"That's what I'm trying to find out." Muhammad tapped the little number above each symbol. Carbon had a 6. Oxygen had an 8. Gold had a 79, which seemed ridiculous for such a small square. He wondered what the numbers were counting. They climbed in a gradual slope across the rows, never repeating, never skipping, like seats being filled one at a time in order. "There has to be a reason they go up like that."

Anderson flipped the sheet over. On the back, Mr. Brennan had written a single question: How many protons are in a neon atom? Nothing else. No hint, no answer.

Muhammad went still. Somewhere in the back of his mind, a sentence from Monday's lesson surfaced like something slowly rising out of water he'd thought was empty. He'd half heard it while doodling, but now it came back whole: an element's atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element. Every atom. Not some atoms, not usually. Every single one. He stared at the paper. Could the numbers up there be the atomic numbers? And if they were, then each number was a count of protons, hidden away in the middle of atoms too small to see, the way a cashier's drawer holds money you can't view from the counter.

"Neon," he said. "Find neon."

Anderson ran his finger along the second row. "Here. Ne. Number ten."

"Ten," Muhammad said slowly, testing the idea like a stone he wasn't sure would hold his weight. "Then every neon atom in the world has ten protons. The neon in signs, the neon in the museum tube Mr. Brennan showed us. Ten, every time." He checked it against another element to be sure the rule wasn't just for gases. Oxygen sat at number 8, and he remembered Mr. Brennan saying oxygen was the element every living organism depended on. Eight protons, then, in every oxygen atom inside every breathing thing on the planet. It gave him a strange, ticklish feeling, like the whole table was whispering a code.

"So the quiz isn't about memorizing numbers at all," Anderson said. "It's about reading the table."

"Right. It tells you." Muhammad grabbed his pencil and wrote the neon answer in his notebook, then underlined it. On the way, he noticed chlorine at 17 and said, "Bet you anything chlorine atoms each have seventeen of these things, and nobody had to count them one by one, because somebody already did." Anderson dunked a chip, and Muhammad turned the sheet back over to hunt for the next question.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Hydrogen has atomic number 1, so every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton.
story:
Quinn's booth had a hand-drawn periodic table pinned to cardboard, and Mr. Rosen, the judge, would reach her table in twenty minutes. The plan had been to quiz visitors, but Akram had just pointed at the crooked corner where a water glass had soaked the poster overnight, and the whole left edge had curled like a dead leaf. "It's ruined," he said. "The judges will think we did the whole project the night before." Andrew, who wanted his name on a winning ribbon more than he wanted lunch, was already pressing the paper flat with both palms.

"We need it to lie flat," Quinn said. She tried tape, but the paper contracted away from the cardboard each time she let go, pulling its corner up like a stubborn flap of wing. Andrew fetched a stack of dictionaries from the lost-and-found shelf while Akram hunted through his backpack for the sturdier clipboard from his volcano project, the durable plastic one that had survived seventh grade and two bus rides.

While they worked, Quinn stared at the numbers she had copied in careful marker along the top row. Each element had a little number above its symbol, and she had never really looked at them before. Hydrogen sat alone in the top left corner with a small 1 printed above the H. "One," she said aloud. Andrew glanced over. "One what?"

"One proton," Quinn said, tracing the H with her finger. "The atomic number is the number of protons." She wasn't sure how she knew it was true, so she tested it. If the number counted protons, then helium, with its 2 in the next box over, would have two protons, and carbon, with its 6, would have six. She checked the key in the library book under her chair, and the key agreed, box after box, all the way down to the heavy metals. The rule held. She felt the way she felt when a combination lock finally clicked open, and she copied a note onto an index card and propped it beside the water glass she used for her demonstration.

Akram leaned in, chewing his pen. "So hydrogen's the simplest one? Just one proton, and that's it?" "Every hydrogen atom has exactly one," Quinn said. He grinned and wrote it on a spare card, then held the card up like a flashcard for his little brother's math drills. "Quiz me. Judge me."

Mr. Rosen arrived four minutes early, while Andrew's dictionaries were still stacked on the corner of the poster and Akram's volcano clipboard was holding down the bottom edge. He looked at the warped table, then at the cards, and asked Quinn to explain the numbers. She walked him from hydrogen in the top left corner down through the rows, her finger steady even where the paper buckled. He nodded twice and made a note on his clipboard.

They did not win. The ribbon went to a boy with a laser and a mirror, and Andrew sat down hard on the folded chair and stared at the floor. Quinn peeled the periodic table off the cardboard, curl and all, and slid it into her folder. On the bus home, Akram tapped her elbow and held up his crumpled flashcard with the H and the 1 on it. "Quiz me again," he said. "One proton."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: The 'butterflies' people feel when nervous come from adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach toward the muscles.
story:
Alexander stood outside the ice cream shop ten minutes early, hands in his pockets, watching the door. Inside, Ms. Wiśniewski from next door was wiping the counter, and the glass case glowed with thirty-one flavors. He had been hungry all afternoon until suddenly, at lunch, he wasn't.

He thought back to the cafeteria. He had taken two bites of his turkey sandwich and set it down, and his stomach had felt hollow and fluttery at the same time. Kael had leaned across the table and looked at him like he was diagnosing a sick machine. "That's butterflies," Kael said. "Adrenaline. It makes your heart speed up and pulls blood away from your stomach toward your muscles." Abdul, on Kael's other side, had nodded solemnly, as if this were a fundamental law of the universe, like gravity. Alexander had pushed his tray away and hoped they were wrong.

Now, waiting, he noticed his heart hammering in his chest, exactly the way Kael had described. His stomach still felt empty and strange. So the fluttery feeling had a real, physical cause, and that meant it might be fixable. He tested a simple idea. If the adrenaline was making his heart accelerate, then slowing everything down might send things back the way they belonged. He sat on the bench by the door, planted his feet, and breathed in for four counts and out for six. Ms. Wiśniewski glanced out the window and gave him a small wave, which he returned.

By the time a girl from his science class came around the corner with her bike helmet under her arm, his pulse had settled to almost normal. "Hi," she said. "You beat me here."

"I got tired of pacing at home," Alexander said, which was close enough to true. They went in together, and every neuron in his brain scrambled to think of something to say, so he pointed at the case instead. "Double chocolate," he said. "Unless you want to split something weird, like mango and pistachio."

She laughed. "Mango and pistachio. Obviously."

They took the first table by the window. He took a spoonful, and the flavor came through bright and clear, because for the first time since noon his stomach felt like an ordinary stomach again. Outside, a sprinkler chattered across the sidewalk, and Ms. Wiśniewski refilled the napkin dispenser without looking up.

"So," the girl said, tapping her spoon against her cone, "movie at seven, or do you want to finish this and just walk to the river first?"

"River first," Alexander said, and stood up with the check in his hand.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Sprinting the first lap faster than a pace you can hold uses up quick anaerobic energy early, so the runner usually slows sharply on the second lap.
story:
Anais stood at the starting line of the park track with Campbell and Caleb and six other kids from Ms. Ahmadi's running club. The race was eight hundred metres, two laps, and Anais had watched Campbell win the trial last week by blasting off the line and holding on. Her plan for today was simpler: count her steps, hold back on lap one, and see what happened.

"Not that again," Campbell said. "You're going to oppose me just to prove a point."

"It's not about you," Anais said. "I want to test something."

The whistle blew. Campbell surged to the front immediately, and Anais let her go. She settled into fourth place and counted, matching her stride to a rhythm she could imagine holding for four more minutes. By the first turn Campbell was ten metres ahead. Anais felt the pull to chase her, the way the whole pack leaned forward as one, and she stayed where she was.

At the end of the first lap, Campbell still led, but the gap had stopped growing. Anais passed Caleb, then the girl in second, and watched Campbell's shoulders rise toward her ears. Her stride shortened. On the back straight of lap two, Campbell's arms dropped and her feet seemed to land heavier, and Anais understood what she had suspected since last week: if you sprint the first lap faster than a pace you can hold, you spend the quick energy early, and the second lap goes badly. Campbell had slowed sharply, exactly like the kids who faded in the race Anais had timed from the fence.

Anais passed her on the final straight, and so did the girl behind Anais. Campbell crossed the line fifth, walked to the grass, and sat down without a word. Anais finished second and bent over, breathing hard but not empty.

Campbell looked up. "I had nothing left. Nothing."

"Now you know," Anais said. "Next time go out slower."

"That wasn't in our negotiation," Campbell said. "You said you were testing a theory, not passing me."

"The theory was about you passing yourself, sort of," Anais said, and offered her hand. "Race me again Thursday. Hold my pace for the first lap and see what you've got left."

Campbell took the hand and pulled herself up. "Thursday," she said, and jogged toward the water fountain with Anais beside her.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Soap breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses, which is one reason washing with soap removes them better than rinsing with water alone.
story:
Amelia sat propped against her pillows with a box of tissues within reach and a cup of warm tea going cold on the nightstand. Three days of flu had left her throat raw and her bedroom looking like a storm had passed through it: crumpled blankets, a stack of unread comics, her water glass catching the afternoon light so it refracted a small rainbow onto the wall. Her little brother wedged himself into the doorway, holding his hands out in front of him like a surgeon.

"I washed," he announced. "Ms. Bondarenko says we have to, since you're sick. But I did it the fast way. Water only." He turned his hands over, pleased with himself.

Amela coughed, then frowned. She had been rinsing with plain water for years herself, back before she got sick, because it was quicker. "Come here," she said. Her voice came out like gravel, but he came. "Water alone doesn't get rid of flu viruses. Soap does."

"That's weird," her brother said. "Soap is just slippery stuff."

"It breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses," Amelia said. "That's why washing with soap removes them better than rinsing with water alone." She had read it on the fact sheet the school nurse sent home, and at the time she'd skimmed past it. Now, with her own forehead still warm, it seemed worth understanding.

She wanted him to actually believe it instead of just nodding, so she tried an experiment. "Go get the dish soap from the kitchen and my little mirror." He galloped off and came back with both. Amelia dabbed a smear of cooking oil onto the mirror with a tissue. "Pretend the oil is the fatty layer around a virus," she rasped. "First, water only." She dripped water onto the oily spot. The drops sat there, beading up, refusing to mix. Her brother poked at the mirror.

"It's just sitting on it. Nothing happened."

"Exactly. Now watch." She added one drop of dish soap and stirred gently with a cotton swab. The oil broke apart into smears and faded, and the water spread flat across the glass. Her brother leaned in until his nose almost touched the mirror.

"Whoa. It fell apart."

"That's what happens to the virus," Amelia said. "It's got that fatty layer around it, and soap tears it open. Water alone can't do that." It struck her that her assumption all these years had been that washing was washing, and that assumption had been wrong. For a pessimistic moment she thought about every doorknob she'd touched with damp, unsoaped hands. Then she pushed the thought away, because her brother was already sprinting toward the bathroom shouting, "I'm going to destroy all the viruses!"

She heard the faucet, then the pump of the soap dispenser, then an enthusiastic twenty-second scrub that her mother would have applauded. Amelia blew her nose, picked up her tea, and watched the little rainbow from her water glass crawl slowly along the wall as the sun sank. From the bathroom came her brother's voice, muffled but triumphant: "Take that, fatty outer layer."

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The treaty gave Poland a strip of land reaching the Baltic Sea, called the Polish Corridor, which cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany.
story:
Christopher stood in front of the giant wall map of Europe, 1919, and frowned. Most of the countries looked roughly like they did in his atlas at home, but one piece of Germany sat all alone on the right side of the page, cut off from the rest like an island with no water around it. He leaned closer and read the label: East Prussia.

"You're blocking the light," Hasan said from behind him.

"Look at this. Why is that bit separated?"

Hasan squinted at the map. "Maybe the map is wrong. Old maps get things wrong." His skepticism was reasonable, Christopher supposed. Museums did contain plenty of stuff that had been corrected later.

But Christopher traced the gap with his finger. A strip of land ran from Poland all the way north to the Baltic Sea, slicing between the main part of Germany and the lonely piece. Whoever drew the map had drawn it that way on purpose. "Maps this big don't get printed with a hole in a country by accident," he said. "Somebody wanted that strip to belong to Poland."

Ms. Chan's class had come to the museum to gather material for their projects on how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War. Christopher had chosen the topic because it sounded easy, one treaty, one war, a straight line between them. Now the line looked crooked. He had read that Germany was angry about the treaty, but until this moment he had never pictured anything concrete to be angry about.

Martin wandered over from the display of old newspapers. "Find anything good?"

"A country split in half by a hallway," Christopher said. He pulled out his phone and photographed the map, then crouched to read the small caption at the bottom edge of the display. It gave the strip a name.

"It's called the Polish Corridor," he read aloud. "The treaty gave Poland a strip of land reaching the Baltic Sea, and it cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany."

Martin stared at the map. "So the people in East Prussia, if they wanted to travel to the rest of Germany, they'd have to cross another country?"

"Or go all the way around by sea, probably. Or through it with papers." Christopher thought about his own street. If a line were drawn through it, and the neighbors on the other side suddenly lived in a different country, he would notice every single day. He had assumed Germany's anger after the treaty was vague, like being mad about losing a game. This wasn't vague. It was drawn on the map, in a shape you could point to.

He sat down on the bench across from the display and started writing on his notepad. His first draft had said the treaty "provoked resentment," which his teacher had marked as too general. Now he wrote a different opening: start with the map, the corridor, the stranded piece of land, and let the reader see the shape of the problem before anyone explained it.

Hasan sat down beside him, still unconvinced. "How do you know the caption isn't oversimplifying?"

"Because the map agrees with it, and the map was made in 1930, before anyone knew what story our textbook wanted to tell." Christopher held up the notepad. "Also, I'm going to ask the docent if they have the actual treaty terms on paper in the archive room. If I'm going to argue this in front of the class, I want it explicit, not just my reading of a wall display."

They found the archive room at the end of the hall, and Christopher filled out the request slip with careful handwriting, then slid it across the desk to the volunteer.

"I'd like to see whatever you have on the Polish Corridor," he said.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft, and fortissimo, written ff, means very loud.
story:
Adam had three days to learn the last page of "March of the Silver Trumpets," and the trumpets were ruining it. Every time the band reached the final phrase, they blasted it like a fire alarm, even though Adam was almost sure the sheet music said otherwise. Ms. Hamdan kept raising her hand and saying, "From measure forty again," until the percussion kids started keeping count of the restarts on a sticky note.

The concert was Friday night, and Adam wanted one thing: to hear the ending sound the way the composer intended, not like a stampede. During lunch he dragged the sheet music to the corner of the band room and squinted at the tiny letters under the final notes. There were two small f's at measure thirty-two, and two small p's at the very end. He remembered a line his cousin had told him once, a random anecdote from her piano lessons: "The markings aren't decoration. Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft, and fortissimo, written ff, means very loud." So the ending was supposed to be very soft, and the trumpets were playing the quiet part like it was the loud part.

He needed proof. Tiana, who played French horn, sat next to the trumpet section, so after school Adam showed her the measures and asked her to watch the trumpets' eyes during the run-through. If they never looked down at the markings, they weren't ignoring them on purpose; they just hadn't seen them. Phoenix, who played snare drum, wanted in too, mostly because he had bet a granola bar that the trumpets couldn't play quietly even if they tried. "I want to win this bet," Phoenix said, "but I also want us not to sound like a dumpster falling down stairs, so it's complicated."

At rehearsal, Tiana reported that the lead trumpet player's eyes had stayed glued to the conductor the whole time. Adam raised his hand before Ms. Hamdan could call measure forty. "Can we try the ending with the dynamics printed on the page?" he asked. "The two little letters under the notes." The lead trumpet player leaned forward, squinted, and said, "Oh. I thought those were typos."

They ran it again. The loud part at measure thirty-two rolled out big and bright, ff as written, and then, instead of getting louder, the whole band dropped to a whisper. The sound felt like it fluctuated between thunder and breath, exactly as the page promised. Ms. Hamdan lowered her baton slowly, and her usually neutral face broke into a grin. Phoenix slid the granola bar across the stand to Tiana. "Fine. They can be quiet. But I want it noted that I predicted the dumpster version."

On Friday, the ending came off so soft that a baby in the third row stopped crying to listen. Adam caught Tiana's eye, and she mouthed, "Two little letters."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
story:
Dear Dad,

You missed a good dinner. Anaeve's mom said I could write and tell you how it went, since you were the one who said I'd never learn to cook anything.

Anaeve and I made pasta sauce from scratch at her house, and Zara came over to supervise, which mostly meant eating crackers and being skeptical about everything. First I had to chop an onion, and Anaeve showed me the claw grip, where you curl your fingertips under and let your knuckles guide the knife. I modified the technique almost immediately by dropping the onion on the floor, but after that I actually did fine, and I still have all ten fingers, which I consider the main victory of the evening. I cried the whole time anyway. Zara said that was the onion's revenge.

Here is the part you'll like. The sauce went into the pot and we let it cook, and we set the table and argued about whether the pasta should be spaghetti or penne. When we tasted the sauce it was thin, more like tomato water with ambitions. Zara suggested adding a whole jar of tomato paste, which Anaeve said would turn it into paste soup. I looked at the pot and noticed something. The lid was on, and the glass was all fogged up with little drops running back down into the sauce. All that water was going up as vapor, hitting the lid, and falling right back in. It was a little onion-water circle, going nowhere.

So I took the lid off and let the sauce keep bubbling with the lid off, so the water could escape as steam instead of dripping back in. Anaeve thought I was ruining it. Mr. Littlechild, the neighbor, had come by to return a ladder, and he leaned in the doorway and said, "Let the boy try it." Twenty minutes later the sauce was thicker and actually tasted like sauce. Zara had seconds. Zara having seconds is like a standing ovation from a very tough crowd.

Anaeve's mom took a photo of the three of us with the empty pot, so expect that in the group chat. Next time I'm going to try garlic, with goggles on.

Your son,
Alexandre

P.S. I am bringing home leftovers in a container labeled DO NOT EAT, which means do not eat them.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running directly behind another runner shelters you from the wind, so following someone on the first lap can save energy for the finish.
story:
The flags on the far goalposts were snapping sideways, and Ruby watched them instead of the starting line. Chad had told her the wind on the back straight was the worst part of the eight hundred metres, worse even than the hill behind the school. "You go out too fast every time," he said, pulling his warmup jacket over his head. "First lap like a rocket, second lap like a shopping cart."

"That's because nobody ever taught me a formula for it," Ruby said.

"You don't need a formula. You need a brain."

Mr. MacLeod, who coached the distance runners on Saturdays, blew his whistle from the fence. "Eight hundred, two laps, Ruby. The race starts on the second lap." That was all he said, and it annoyed her, because it wasn't an instruction. It was a riddle.

The whistle went, and Ruby did what she always did: she sprinted. Campbell, who usually beat her by three or four seconds, slid in front of her on the first bend, and Ruby locked onto the bouncing ponytail and followed. When they hit the back straight the wind hit too, a cold shove that pushed at her chest and made her eyes water. Ruby felt it on her shoulders and her arms, everywhere except the space directly behind Campbell, where the air arrived soft and strange, as if someone had shut a door. She thought, so that's what the riddle means. She stayed close through the bend, matching stride for stride, saving something she couldn't see but could feel in her legs, like money in a pocket.

The bell rang for the second lap, and Campbell faded, exactly like Chad had faded last week and Ruby had faded the week before. Ruby went around her on the final bend, and her legs still had spring in them, actual spring, and she crossed the line four seconds ahead of her best time. Campbell finished and bent over, hands on knees, gulping air. Ruby got her water bottle and held it out, because Campbell looked worse than Ruby had ever looked losing.

"How," Campbell wheezed.

"You were the windbreak," Ruby said. "I hid behind you the whole back straight. Running behind someone shelters you from the wind. You gave me the finish." Chad jogged over, and Ruby was already planning, because the city meet was in two weeks and she would need to acquire a rival smart enough to lead the first lap and strong enough to deserve following. She looked at Chad and grinned. "You," she said. "You're leading me for one lap at the meet, and I'm buying the pizza after."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The number of protons decides which element an atom is: any atom with eight protons is oxygen, and an atom with seven protons is nitrogen.
story:
Ava had the periodic table taped to the kitchen wall, but the numbers kept sliding off her brain like water off a duck's back. The quiz was tomorrow morning, first period, and Ms. Rajapakse had promised it would include the tricky question from last week, the one half the class got wrong. Ava flopped onto the kitchen chair and glared at the chart. "You don't even look that complicated," she told it.

Her phone buzzed. It was Aleena: "Still studying? I am LOST. What even is an atomic number?" Ava typed back, "It's the small number on each box." Then she paused, because that answer felt like the outside of a locked door. She knew the number sat there, but she didn't know what it did. She pulled her notebook closer and started copying boxes onto index cards, one element per card, hiding the atomic number with a folded sticky note so she could quiz herself.

Her mother came through with a grocery bag and set a carton of strawberries beside her. "Brain food," she said quietly, and Ava noticed her mom's hands were cold from the bike ride, so she got up and made tea without being asked. While the kettle heated, she flipped the first card. Oxygen. She lifted the sticky note a corner at a time, like lifting a blind. Number eight. "Okay, oxygen, you're an eight," she said. The next card, nitrogen, turned out to be seven. She frowned. Seven and eight, side by side in the second row of the chart, neighbors, almost like siblings.

Then she remembered the question from class. Ms. Rajapakse had asked what would happen if an oxygen atom somehow lost a proton, and almost everyone said it would still be oxygen, just lighter. The answer had surprised the whole room: it would not be oxygen anymore. It would be nitrogen. Ava sat down so fast she knocked her pencil to the floor. So the number wasn't just a label stuck on the outside. The number was the thing itself. Eight protons meant oxygen, and seven meant nitrogen, and if that count changed, the element changed with it. Nobody had explained it to her. She had walked straight into it, the way you walk into a glass door you didn't know was there.

She texted Aleena: "Forget memorizing. The atomic number tells you how many protons. Eight protons, you've got oxygen. Seven, nitrogen. That's the whole secret." The kettle shrieked and her mother called that the tea was getting volatile sitting there boiling, so Ava poured two cups and carried one over. She tested her idea out loud, since her mother was the only ambassador from the land of people who had finished school long ago. "If an atom has eight protons," Ava asked, "what is it?" Her mom sipped, thought, and said, "Oxygen. From the way you just lit up, anyway."

Ava kept drilling after dinner, flipping cards, guessing, checking. Once she tried to skip a card she'd already missed twice, and felt that would violate her own new rule, so she went back. By ten o'clock she could take any element in the first two rows and say its proton count before she lifted the paper.

In the morning, Ms. Rajapakse's quiz had the question on it, word for word: what happens if an oxygen atom loses a proton? Ava wrote, "It becomes nitrogen," and underlined it. When the papers came back, Selina leaned across the aisle and whispered, "How did you get that one?" Ava slid her periodic table out of her binder, the one with the folded sticky notes still stuck to it, and said, "Flip it over. I'll show you."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The simple interest formula is I = P x r x t: interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years.
story:
Quinn spread the bank flyer across the kitchen table next to her dad's toolbox, because the toolbox meant he was fixing the boiler again and would be too busy to answer questions. "Two accounts," she said to Blakely, who was sitting on the counter eating crackers. "Simple interest and compound interest. Same rate, five years."

"Pick the one with the bigger number at the end," Blakely said. "Easy."

"Except the flyer doesn't show the end. It shows the rate." Quinn stabbed the paper with her pencil. "That's like knowing the piston moves but not where it goes." Down in the basement something clanged, and her dad yelled up that if the foam wrap didn't insulate the pipe by tonight they'd have no hot water for school.

Quinn found the simple one first. She remembered the formula from Mr. Van Dijk's class, the way he'd written it huge across the board: I equals P times r times t. Interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years. She wrote it at the top of her page. Her principal was the two hundred dollars from her birthday. The yearly rate was five percent. The number of years was five. Two hundred times five percent times five. Her pencil flew: that came to fifty dollars of interest, so two hundred fifty at the end. She circled it twice.

"The compound one's the problem," she said. "Every year the interest joins the pile, so I can't just multiply once." She did it the slow way, year by year, chewing her pencil and crossing things out. First year, ten dollars. Second year the ten earned its own ten's worth. By year three she was grinning, and by year five she leaned back so fast she nearly knocked Blakely off the counter.

"Twenty-seven dollars more," Quinn said. "Compound wins by twenty-seven whole dollars."

Blakely slid off the counter and looked at the two circled numbers. "So the bank put the small one in big print on the front."

"And the big one in the tiny print on the back." Quinn texted a photo of her page to Mr. Van Dijk, then checked the phone every thirty seconds while she cleared the crackers. When it buzzed, she held it out so Blakely could read it. "Checked your arithmetic," it said. "Both accounts. All correct."

Quinn pumped her fist. Then she grabbed the flyer and marched toward the stairs, calling down to her dad that after the pipe was fixed she needed him to drive her to the bank before it closed.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A null hypothesis is the statement that there is no relationship between the things being studied, which an experiment then tries to reject.
story:
Dylan counted the bean plants on the back counter of the science classroom. Eight pots, four labeled with a music note and four labeled with a plain X. He had set them up eleven days ago, and now Ms. Janssen wanted results by Friday, which meant he needed something to say today.

"Let me guess," said Jazlyn, leaning over his shoulder. "The music ones are taller."

"They're not." Dylan held a ruler against the closest plant in the music group. Nine centimeters. The pot beside it, no music, measured ten. "Brixton said music makes plants grow faster. He heard it from his cousin."

"So he's wrong."

"I don't know yet. That's the problem." Dylan flipped open his notebook, where he had been hiding his confusion behind messy charts, trying to conceal the fact that he had no idea what conclusion to write. If the music plants weren't taller, maybe he'd measured wrong. Maybe the grow lights were uneven. Maybe eleven days wasn't long enough. Any of those could be true, and he couldn't tell them apart by staring at bean sprouts.

Jazlyn picked up a pot and frowned at the soil. "It's really humid under these lights. Maybe that matters more than the music."

"Everything might matter more than the music. That's what I keep thinking." Dylan tapped his pencil against the counter. Then he stopped. "Wait. Maybe that's the answer. Maybe the thing to prove isn't that music helps. Maybe the thing to prove is that it does nothing."

Jazlyn set the pot down. "How do you prove nothing?"

"You describe what nothing looks like first. Like, the music plants and the quiet plants grow the same amount. Then if the numbers don't match that, the music did something." He wrote fast, before the idea could slip away. "Brixton was telling me his sister did this in high school. She called it a null hypothesis." He looked up. "That's the statement that there's no relationship between the things being studied, and the experiment tries to reject it. Brixton's exact words. He texted them to me at eleven at night."

"Rejecting nothing. Sure. Normal science." Jazlyn grabbed the ruler. "Measure. I'll write."

They worked down the row, calling out numbers. When they finished, Dylan added both columns. The music group averaged 9.2 centimeters. The quiet group averaged 9.4. Almost identical. He leaned back so fast his stool tipped, and he grabbed the edge of the counter just as Brixton walked in carrying two balloons left over from the assembly, one half-deflated.

"Whoa," Brixton said. "You look like you saw a ghost."

"Worse. My data agrees with you." Dylan spun the notebook around. "Null hypothesis holds. So far."

Brixton put a balloon to his mouth and blew, watching the inflation with great ceremony. "So what you're saying is, I was right for the wrong reason."

"I'm saying I can't reject you yet," Dylan said. "Which is the nicest thing anyone's ever said in this classroom."

"Friday," Jazlyn reminded them, pointing at the calendar with the ruler. "More data, less gloating."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce an irritating gas, which reaches the eyes and makes them water.
story:
Paige stood in the produce section with her mother's list in her hand, trying to categorize everything into meals before they got home. Soup night, taco night, pasta night. Soup night needed onions, and onion shopping had become personal. Last week she had chopped one for her mother's stew and ended up crying so hard at the counter that her mother thought something had happened at school. "It was the onion," Paige had insisted, wiping her face with a dish towel. A vegetable had defeated her, and she wanted to know how.

She picked up two yellow onions and turned one over in her palm. It looked so innocent. How could something sealed up and silent do all that? She was still wondering about it when she spotted Rhea by the bread aisle, shopping with her grandmother. Rhea came over, and Paige told her the whole story, ending with, "I actually cried. Full tears. Over a vegetable."

"That's a thing," Rhea said. "My grandma cries every time she cooks. She says our family recipes are hereditary, but so are the tears, apparently." Rhea leaned in like she was sharing a secret. "Maci told me cutting an onion breaks open its cells and lets out stuff inside that makes a gas, and the gas floats up into your eyes. That's why they water. It's not sadness, it's gas."

Paige stared at the onion in her hand. A gas, from inside the cells, traveling to her eyes. So it had a route, and routes could be blocked. She turned the idea over all the way to the checkout and then through the front door of her apartment, where she laid out her ingredients on the counter like a scientist laying out equipment. If the gas reached her eyes from the cut surface, then maybe fewer cuts meant less gas at once. Maybe a sharper knife would break fewer cells than a dull one. Maybe cold slowed things down. She had a fridge, a knife block, and three theories.

She put one onion in the freezer for ten minutes and left the other on the counter, then sharpened the big knife until it slid through a sheet of paper towel she held up to test it. Her mother drifted through the kitchen, raised an eyebrow at the stopwatch on Paige's phone, and said only, "Dinner's at seven." Paige set the cold onion on the cutting board and pressed the blade down through its center, eyes wide open, watching and waiting.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Relationship researcher John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which is about one specific action, from criticism, which attacks a person's character with words like 'you always' or 'you never'.
story:
The trouble started at the monkey bars, where Ahmad had told Sam what Norah said about the science fair groups on Friday, and now half the class knew she thought the team picking order was unfair. "You never keep secrets," Norah said, and Ahmad's face went stiff, and he walked off toward the fence. She stood there with her fists tight, watching him kick gravel along the chain-link, and the bell would ring in eleven minutes, which was all the time left before lunch ended and they'd have to sit through the whole afternoon not speaking.

"You never," Mr. Quinn said mildly, pausing by the swings with his coffee. "Harsh words, those." He moved on before she could answer, and Norah turned it over in her head. It was true that Ahmad had told Sam, but "you never keep secrets" was a bigger thing than that, and it wasn't even true, because he had kept the secret about her haircut disaster for three whole weeks last spring. She began to suspect that the size of the sentence was the problem, not the truth of it. Maybe there was a rule: a complaint about one specific thing lands differently than an attack on the whole person.

She had a plan to test it, and only ten minutes to do it. She ran across the playground, past Maxim, who was trying to organize the four-square hierarchy and kept chanting the rankings like the order mattered more than breathing. "Move up or move down," he called, but she dodged around the square.

Ahmad was leaning on the fence. Norah took a breath and forced the words out in their smallest form. "You told Sam what I said on Friday. That's the specific thing I'm mad about. Not 'you always,' not 'you never.' Just Friday." Ahmad looked at the gravel, then at her. "That's actually fair," he said. "I did tell Sam. I was mad you got picked first and I didn't, because I envy how easy group things are for you, and I wanted to knock you down a notch. That was naive of me, it just made everything worse." He scuffed his shoe in the dirt. "I'm sorry about Friday."

"You could have just complained about it," Norah said. "A complaint is about one thing. What you did and what I did, those were bigger, like saying the person is bad instead of the action." Ahmad nodded slowly, like something was settling into place behind his eyes. The bell rang across the yard, and Maxim abandoned his kingdom mid-shout, and the players scattered toward the doors, and Ahmad held the chain-link gate open for her. "Lunch tomorrow?" he asked. "I'll tell you about the Sam conversation, all of it, from the start."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: If a quoted line is a question, the question mark goes inside the quotation marks and the tag after it starts with a lowercase letter, as in "Where are you?" he asked.
story:
Maeva slid her draft across the library table until it bumped Merrick's elbow. "Read the part where the diver finds the door," she said. The radiator under the window ticked like a slow clock, and somewhere behind the biography shelves Aliza was muttering lines from her own story about a haunted aquarium.

Merrick read, and his frown appeared before his words did. "You wrote, 'He asked' with a capital H. Right there, after the question. That's what Mr. Njoroge circled on my paper last week." He tapped the sentence: "Where are you going?" He asked. "The H is wrong. I don't get it. There's a question mark there, so something new must start."

Maeva stared at the mark. It sat inside the quotation marks, snug against the final word, and she tried to picture what the punctuation was actually doing. Maybe the marks were like a box around the spoken words, she thought, and the question mark belonged in the box because the words themselves were the question. The tag afterward, the "he asked" part, was just a handle on the outside. A handle wasn't the start of anything new. "Try it lowercase," she said, mostly to test the idea out loud. "'Where are you going?' he asked." She said it both ways, and the lowercase version sounded smoother, like the tag was leaning on the quote instead of standing apart.

"Every single time?" Merrick asked. "Even if it's the best question in the story?"

"Every time it's a question inside the quotes. The question mark goes inside, and the tag after it starts lowercase."

Aliza appeared from behind the shelves, carrying her notebook like a tray. "Fixing dialogue again? That's becoming a ritual with you two." She dropped into the chair and pointed at Maeva's page. "My climax is still mush. The diver opens the door and then I just, I don't know, describe the water."

"That's because nothing peaks," Maeva said. She read Aliza's paragraph and felt the problem like a flat hallway with no door at the end. Last term she had made the same mistake, she remembered, burying her best moment in the middle of a description of weather, and Mr. Njoroge had written "save it for the top" in green ink. She had been annoyed then. Now she was grateful, though she still wasn't sure she'd have chosen green ink.

She borrowed Aliza's pen and drew a small mountain in the margin, an arrow at the peak. "Put the door-opening there. Last paragraph. Let her say something right at the top, one question that changes everything." Aliza chewed her pen and then wrote fast, hunched over the table, and when she read the new ending aloud her voice dropped to a whisper at the right spot.

Merrick copied the corrected sentence into his own draft, muttering the rule twice like a spell. "One objective for the weekend," he said. "No capital letters after question marks. I'm going to find every one."

Maeva smiled and looked at her page again. The lowercase h sat there, small and correct, and the radiator ticked on. She underlined the diver's final line twice. "What's behind it?" she asked.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
Florence stood on Penny's front step holding a box of oranges wrapped in a dish towel, because Penny had called an hour ago in a panic. "My exchange student's grandparents are visiting tonight, and my mom delegated all the Japanese customs to me," Penny had said. "You're coming, right? Dinner's at six sharp. They flew in from Kyoto this morning, and they're only here one night." That gave Florence exactly four hours to stop feeling like the most clueless person on the street.

Penny opened the door before Florence knocked. "Okay, so, shoes off," she whispered, pointing at a row of slippers by the mat. Florence unlaced her sneakers and set them neatly beside the grandfather's polished black shoes, which sat with their toes pointing toward the door instead of toward the hall. She filed that detail away, the way she filed away the smell of rice steam drifting from the kitchen and the small vase of three chrysanthemums on the table.

The grandparents rose when Florence came in. The grandmother bowed, a slow dip from the waist, not too deep. Florence's dilemma hit her instantly. Should she bow back the same amount, or more, or less? She had no idea, and guessing wrong in front of guests felt like tripping on the welcome mat. She matched the grandmother's bow exactly, and the old woman's eyes crinkled warmly.

Then Penny's little brother barrelled in and gave the grandfather an enormous wave and a fist bump. The grandfather laughed and returned a bow so shallow it was barely a nod. Florence watched, chewing her lip. That was the clue she needed. The grandmother's bow had been deeper and longer than that nod, and the grandfather had clearly done the small one on purpose, playful, casual. So the depth and the length of a bow meant something. The longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it showed. She tested it at dinner, when the grandmother handed her a bowl of rice with both hands and Florence bowed low and slow before accepting it. The grandmother bowed even lower in return, and Penny's mom shot Florence a look of pure gratitude across the table.

Florence also noticed she was the only one slurping nothing. The grandfather drew his noodles in with cheerful, ringing slurps, so she tried it too, quietly at first, and he grinned and slurped louder, which made Penny's brother laugh so hard he nearly knocked over his tea. Later, when Florence unwrapped her oranges and offered the dish towel as part of the gift, the grandmother insisted on wrapping the towel back around an empty bowl for Florence to carry home, saying it should never be empty, and Penny translated while grinning.

At the door, the grandfather turned and bowed, deep and long this time, holding it for several seconds. Florence understood what that meant now, and she returned it with the same slow care, until Penny nudged her and whispered, "Okay, that's enough, he's going to think you're stuck."

"He can think I'm stuck," Florence said. "Some people deserve a long bow."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
The banner was supposed to be finished by five o'clock, and it still said only one word, diaspora, in tall purple letters across the top. Ariana stood in Maina's garage with a paintbrush in her hand, staring at it. The cultural festival was Saturday, and Maina's family was hosting a table about their community, but when Ariana had asked what the banner word meant, Maina had just shrugged.

"I copied it off my grandmother's flyer," Maina admitted. "She's at work. Skylar's coming over with the dictionary from school, but that thing is older than Mr. Romano." Skylar arrived with the dictionary and also with pizza, which meant nobody opened the dictionary for a while. The garage smelled like cardboard and tomato sauce, and the blank half of the banner waited.

It was Skylar who finally thumbed to the D section. "Diaspora. From a Greek word meaning scattering," she read. "It describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors." Maina set down her pizza slice very slowly. "Scattering," she repeated, like she was tasting the word. "My grandma always says her family scattered like seeds. I thought she was just being dramatic." Ariana remembered something then, a flashback rising up whole: her own grandfather at the kitchen table, tracing a route on a map with his finger, saying that his village existed only in stories now because everyone had left it. She had been eight and had thought he was talking about gardening.

Ariana tested her idea out loud. "So a diaspora isn't a place. It's people. It's the scattering itself, and living far away from where your ancestors came from." Skylar pointed at the banner. "Then the word isn't just decoration. It's the whole point of the table." Maina grabbed the paints and, in quick strokes, drew seeds blowing from one side of the banner to the other, each seed turning into a small house. It was better than anything they had planned.

That night Maina's grandmother came home, exhausted from her shift, and Ariana watched her go still in front of the banner. She didn't praise the drawings. She touched the seeds and then, quietly, she began to confide in them, telling how her mother had been a farmer and had carried seeds in her apron pocket across an ocean, because agriculture was all she knew, and losing the land had left her feeling more vulnerable than the crossing itself. Maina wrote it all down on a card for the table.

Saturday came, and the festival filled the gym with food and drumming. Ariana stood behind the table feeling proud, until a woman stopped, read the card, and frowned at Maina's grandmother. "You shouldn't put our losses on display like this," the woman said, and walked off. The grandmother slid the card into her apron pocket, next to her keys, exactly where the seeds used to go, and said, "Well. Scattered again."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: More than 200 different viruses can cause the common cold, and rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause.
story:
Lucas had been on the couch for two days with a box of tissues, a blanket, and a notebook he was too tired to write in. His throat felt like sandpaper, and he despised being sick more than he despised anything else, mostly because it was boring. He was missing the science fair meeting, and Ms. Novák had said this week was the last chance to lock in a topic before the deadline. His phone buzzed. It was Emery.

"you alive?" the message said. Lucas typed back that he was alive but full of virus. Then he stopped. Which virus, though? He'd had a flu shot in the fall, and his mom had said, see, you're covered. But here he was, coughing anyway. He dragged his laptop over and searched why there is no vaccine for the common cold. The answer that came up made him sit up straight. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold, and the most frequent cause was a group called rhinoviruses. He read the sentence twice. Two hundred. A flu shot covered a handful of strains, and colds were a whole crowd.

He called Emery. "Guess how many viruses give you a cold," Lucas said, before Emery could even say hello.

"I don't know, like five?"

"More than 200 different viruses. And the most frequent ones are called rhinoviruses."

"No wonder we get colds all the time," Emery said. There was a pause, and Lucas heard typing in the background, which meant Emery was only half listening. "So, um. The science fair thing. Ms. Novák picked lab partners today. You got me, obviously. But I already told her our topic. Is that okay? I mean, you're not mad?"

Lucas realized Emery hadn't texted to check on him at all. Emery had texted because he felt guilty. "What topic?" Lucas asked.

"Vaccines," Emery said quickly. "How they work. It's a legitimate project, it has real research, I checked. And now you're literally an expert because you looked all that stuff up while dying on your couch." Emery laughed a little, then stopped, waiting.

Lucas thought about it. A vaccine project with a partner who had already chosen it wasn't what he'd planned. But two hundred viruses was a real hook, a question a judge couldn't guess the answer to. "Fine," he said. "But I want the part where we explain why nobody's ever cured the cold. And you owe me all the notes from today's meeting."

"Deal," Emery said. "I'll bring them over tomorrow. My mom says soup helps, so I'm bringing soup. From the corporation-sized can, so don't worry, there's plenty."

"Bring crackers too," Lucas said, and pulled his notebook closer to start a page titled with a fat number: 200.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment, so their expectations cannot sway the results.
story:
Emily spread her science fair notebook across the library table and tapped the page titled "Can People Tell Name-Brand Cola from Store Brand?" The taste test was in three days, and she still had one column blank.

"Twenty people," Alexandre said, reading over her shoulder. "Ten get the name brand first, ten get the store brand. You write down what they say."

"That's the problem." Emily turned her pencil over and over. "What if they guess right just because of how I hand them the cup? If I smile when I give them the good one, that's a clue."

Kaley slid into the third chair with her backpack still on one shoulder. "So don't smile."

"Faces leak," Emily said. "Everything leaks. The way you pour it. Which cup you reach for first."

Mr. Han, the librarian, came by with the cart of returns. He paused at the word "leak." "Testing people?" he asked.

"Taste test," Alexandre said. "For the science fair. My cousin did one last year, and every single person guessed right. He said his brand was just better."

"Was it?" Emily asked.

Alexandre shrugged. "He poured it for them. He wanted his brand to win, so who knows how he poured it."

Emily wrote "cousin" in the margin and crossed it out. She stared at the two columns on her page, one labeled "sample" and one labeled "what they said." Then she drew a third column and labeled it "who knew."

"What if I don't know which cup is which either?" she said slowly. "Then I can't give anything away, because I don't have anything to give."

Kaley frowned. "Then how do you keep track?"

"Someone labels them and leaves." Emily's pencil moved fast now. "My mom pours the cups tonight. She puts a mark on the bottom, like A and B, and writes down which is which on a card. She seals the card in an envelope. Tomorrow she's not even at the fair. She complies with the rule that she can't be in the room when people taste."

"She won't like that rule," Kaley said.

"She'll like it fine. It's for science."

Alexandre took the envelope idea further. "The people tasting can't know either," he said. "If they think the name brand is in one specific cup, they'll believe they taste it, even if it isn't there."

"So nobody knows," Emily said. "Not them, not me. Only the envelope." She flipped to the back of her notebook and found the term in a book she'd read about medicine trials. "It's called double-blind. Neither the participants nor the researchers know who's getting the real thing."

"Then your cousin's test wasn't fair," Alexandre said.

"His test was a story about one person. Mine will be a claim with evidence." She underlined the last line of her plan.

On Saturday she set up her table near the biography section, with its quiet rows and the smell of old paper. The two coolers sat side by side in perfect symmetry, each with plain white cups, and Emily served sample after sample without a clue in her head about what she was pouring. A man in a跑步 jacket tasted cup A, then cup B, and said the store brand was the name brand, absolutely certain. A girl Emily's age got both right. By noon, fourteen of twenty-two people had guessed wrong, which was close to what pure chance would look like.

At two o'clock Mr. Han cut open the envelope with the library's scissors and read the card aloud. Emily tallied the final score: nine right out of twenty-two. She looked at the number for a long moment, then laughed out loud in the middle of the quiet library.

"So nobody could tell," Alexandre said. "Not even you."

"Not even me," Emily said, and wrote it down.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: In a fire, smoke and heat rise, so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor, which is why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke.
story:
The bus smelled like sunscreen and pretzels by the time it reached Old Fort Hastings, where a guide in a tri-corner hat was waiting to show them the barracks, the powder room, and the guard tower. Jaxson had been skeptical about the whole trip, mostly because the permission slip mentioned a fire safety drill, which sounded like something for little kids. "Thirteen years old," he muttered to Jaya as they filed through the gate, "and they're teaching us how to duck."

The surprise came in the guard tower's lower chamber, where a firefighter had set up a machine that pushed out a harmless gray haze, like fog escaping a cooler. The plan was for each student to cross the room through the haze and reach the far door. Hailey went first, walking upright, coughing and waving her arms the moment she hit the wall of gray. The room filled fast, and the haze hung thick near the ceiling while a thinner layer drifted at knee height. Jaxson watched from the line and noticed something: the fog rolled upward when it came out, piling along the top of the room first.

He turned the observation over while the line crept forward. In a real fire, he reasoned, the hot air would act like that machine's fog, carrying smoke upward, which would leave the lower air clearer and cooler than the air above it. That would explain why the drill wanted them low, and it refuted his earlier theory that crawling was just about staying under the smoke's height like limbo. It wasn't only about height. It was about which air was cleaner and cooler, near the floor, where the smoke and heat hadn't pooled.

When his turn came, he stood up straight for exactly three steps, just to test it. His eyes stung and he tasted something acrid, and the heat of the demonstration lamps near the ceiling pressed down on him like a hand. He dropped to his hands and knees and the world changed at once. Below the haze he could see the floorboards, the door frame, even Jaya's sneakers ahead of him. The air felt cooler there too. He crawled fast, and when he pushed through the door he was grinning instead of coughing.

Mr. Bakker met them on the tower steps, clipboard in hand. "Well, Mr. Stand-Up-Straight," he said. "Learn anything in there?"

"Smoke and heat rise," Jaxson said, "so the cleaner, cooler air is down near the floor. That's why you crawl low under it." He looked back at the doorway, where Hailey was still blinking the sting out of her eyes. He jogged up the steps, unclipped his own water bottle, and held it out to her.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
story:
Zoe curled her fingers into what the cookbook called the claw grip, knuckles forward, and set the blade against the onion. "If I cut myself," she said, "I want it noted that I opposed this project from the start."

"You proposed this project," said Kristopher from his perch on the dilapidated stool by the window, the one that wobbled like it was deciding whether to keep being a stool. "On Tuesday. In writing. There was a list."

There had been a list. Number three was "make pasta sauce from scratch, not from a jar," and Zoe had underlined it twice, which at the time had felt like commitment. Now the onion was making her eyes stream and Kristopher was reading out her own list back to her, which she felt was a misuse of the document.

She got through the onion, uneven cubes sliding across the cutting board, and dumped it into the pan with the garlic and a glug of oil. She turned the heat to high because high seemed faster. The kitchen smelled good for about ninety seconds. Then it smelled like something had gone wrong in a way she couldn't see. The sauce, when she stirred and tasted it, was bitter, a flat acrid taste that no amount of stirring fixed.

Kristopher tasted it too and made a face he tried to hide, badly. "It's a new genre of sauce," he said. "Sauce, but punishing."

Zoe stood over the pan and thought. The onion looked fine, soft and golden. She fished out a piece of garlic and looked at it. Dark. Really dark, almost brown at the edges, while the onion beside it had barely colored. They'd gone into the pan at the same moment, on the same heat, and only one of them had burnt. The garlic was in smaller pieces, sure, but Kristopher's onions on taco night got smaller than that and never turned bitter. So maybe it wasn't size. Maybe garlic just couldn't take the heat the way onion could, and it burnt while the onion was still softening, and burnt garlic was what the whole pot now tasted like.

She dumped the batch, rinsed the pan, and started over. This time the onion went in alone, and she waited, scraping and turning, until the pieces went soft and translucent. Only then did she mince the garlic and slide it in, stirring fast. Thirty seconds later the smell was completely different, warm and sweet instead of sharp.

She dropped in the tomatoes, lowered the heat, and handed Kristopher the wooden spoon. "Taste in ten minutes," she said. "And if it's good, we're crediting me twice on that list."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: A young child can drown in just a few inches of water and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath.
story:
Sophia had babysat plenty of times before, but never for the Hendersons' little boy, Eli, who was almost two. Mrs. Henderson showed her where the diapers were, where the snacks were, and then pointed at the upstairs hallway. "Bath is at seven. He loves his ducks."

At seven, Eli sat in the tub with three rubber ducks and about four inches of water, slapping the surface and shrieking with joy. Sophia knelt beside him on the bath mat, keeping one hand on his slippery shoulder. Downstairs, the phone rang. She glanced at the door, then back at Eli, who was reaching for the soap.

Her mother had drilled one rule into her before she ever watched a child: a toddler can drown in just a few inches of water, and it can happen without any splashing or crying out, so a child should never be left alone in or near the bath. Not for a phone call, not for anything. Sophia had rolled her eyes at the time, but standing there with the phone ringing and Eli wobbling forward on his knees, the rule suddenly felt like the edge of a frontier, and she had no idea what lay past it. She was not going to find out.

She yanked the big frog towel off the hook, lifted Eli out of the water even though he protested in a small, furious voice, and wrapped him up like a burrito. Then she carried him, dripping and squirming, down the stairs. "I know," she told him. "Bath is fun. We'll go back." She answered the phone on the fifth ring. It was Mrs. Henderson, checking in.

"Everything okay? I heard the water running."

"Yes, we're in the middle of bath time," Sophia said, bouncing Eli on her hip. "He's taking a break in a towel. He's never alone near the water, not even for a second. That's my rule."

There was a pause, and then a warm sound on the line. "Good girl. That's exactly right."

After the call, Sophia lugged Eli back up and set him on the bathroom floor while she added a little warm water. He was small and still so frail compared to his big sister, Madelyn, who lived next door and sometimes carried him around like a sack of potatoes. Sophia had texted Madelyn earlier: "First night with your brother's twin, the Henderson kid." Madelyn had replied with three laughing faces.

When Eli was dry and in pajamas, Sophia read him the book about the moon three times. On the third time he fell asleep against her arm, one duck still clutched in his fist. She lowered him into the crib the way she had practiced with a pillow an hour before Mrs. Henderson left.

When the headlights swept the front window, Sophia was downstairs writing a note about how many duck books they had read. Mrs. Henderson came in quietly, read it, and smiled. "I have to confess something," she whispered. "I left the phone ringing on purpose. It was a test."

Sophia stared at her. "You did not."

"I did. And you carried him out wrapped in a towel." Mrs. Henderson set her keys in the dish by the door. "Same time next Friday?"

Sophia grinned and picked up her backpack. "Only if the ducks come too."

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: When the monsoon arrives late or brings too little rain, rice planting is delayed and harvests can shrink, which can push food prices up.
story:
The trail climbed in switchbacks above the creek, and Evelyn kept her phone in her pocket, which was hard, because her whole science grade was living inside it. She had a presentation due Monday about monsoons, and so far her notes said only "WIND? + RAIN? + RICE???"

"Are you muttering at the dirt again?" Penelope asked, catching up. "Because the dirt can't help you."

"It's not dirt, it's evidence." Evelyn pointed at the hillside, where the grass had gone crunchy and yellow in patches. "The creek's low, the grass is brittle. That's what happens when the rain comes late."

Santino swung his water bottle by its strap. "So your presentation is about dry grass."

"It's about monsoons." She had read the word a dozen times and still couldn't quite picture it. "In South Asia, the wind changes direction in summer and it pours rain for months. But last year the monsoon came late, and it was weak, so..." She stopped. "Wait. If the rain is late and small, the farmers can't plant their rice on time."

"Boo, rice," Santino said. "Rice is boring."

"That's what I thought too," Evelyn admitted. "But then my mom bought rice on Tuesday and stood in the aisle making a face at the price. It had gone up since last month. She said the news mentioned the weak monsoon, and I thought, that can't be a coincidence."

Ms. Liu, walking at the back of the group, raised an eyebrow but said nothing, which was her way of saying keep going.

Evelyn crouched by the creek and wet her finger, then held it up. Penelope copied her, and so did Santino, though he looked like he was saluting something.

"What are we doing?" Penelope asked.

"Feeling which way the wind blows. If the wind pivots, like it does when a monsoon starts, it comes from a different direction than before. I want to feel a pivot." She closed her eyes. The breeze slid past her wet finger from the uphill side. "Okay. From the ridge. If it pivoted tomorrow and blew from the creek side instead, that would be the kind of switch that pulls moisture in."

Santino frowned at his own finger. "Mine feels cold from every direction."

"That's because you dipped your whole hand in the creek, genius," Penelope said.

Evelyn laughed, then sat down on a rock and started writing fast: late monsoon means delayed planting, weak monsoon means smaller harvest, smaller harvest means the rice costs more, which is why her mom had made the face.
