It was like a chain, and you couldn't see the first link from a grocery store. You had to reason backward, from a price sticker all the way to a wind that pivots an ocean away.

"You're muttering again," Penelope said.

"I'm drafting. It's different."

On the hike down, Santino kept asking questions. Did the farmers just wait? Could they store water to conserve it for a bad year? Was there any crop that handled a late monsoon better? Evelyn answered what she could and wrote down the rest. "Rice isn't boring," Santino announced at the trailhead. "Rice is a whole detective story."

That night she rehearsed the presentation in the kitchen, using a squirt bottle as the ocean, and her dad applauded with a sandwich in one hand.

Monday morning, she stood up in class with her diagrams, took a breath, and said, "My topic is dry grass."

Ms. Liu said, "Evelyn."

"Monsoons," Evelyn said. "I was testing you. Anyway, it starts with a price sticker."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: Japji Sahib is also recited at the Sikh Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar.
story:
Sydney stood in the shoe-lined hallway of the gurdwara with her phone in her pocket, turned off like Ms. Cho had asked, and tried to get the first line of Japji Sahib to stick in her head. Her best friend Larissa was being initiated next month, and she had asked Sydney to help her learn the morning prayer by heart before then. That was a bigger job than Sydney had expected. The words were in Gurmukhi script, and even in the English transliteration they rolled and folded in ways her tongue kept tripping over.

They sat cross-legged on the carpeted floor of the langar hall after the morning service, a shared notebook open between them. "Okay, from Ik Onkar," Larissa said, closing her eyes. She got through four lines, then her memory dropped off a cliff. She opened one eye. "Your turn to catch me."

Sydney had noticed something while listening that morning. The recitation hadn't been one flat string of sound. Certain phrases came back again and again, the way a chorus returns in a song, and the people reciting grew louder and steadier each time. She wondered if the prayer had a shape she couldn't see from the outside, some hierarchy of parts, with the repeated lines holding the smaller ones together. "Do the parts that repeat come at regular intervals?" she asked. "Like, is it consistent?"

Larissa counted on her fingers along the printed page, tapping each heading. "Sunhil, sunh," she murmured, tapping, tapping. "Yeah. The sections all end with the same kind of closing phrase." She looked up, surprised at her own discovery, as if the pattern had been hiding in her mouth all those years of listening and only now showed itself.

They drilled the first five sections that way, with Sydney tapping the carpet at every returning phrase like a metronome. It worked better than plain repetition. When Larissa could say all five without dropping a word, they went to find Ms. Cho, who was stacking steel cups in the kitchen. "She's ready for the whole thing," Sydney said.

Ms. Cho smiled and dried her hands. "Do you know why we take extra care with Japji Sahib?" she asked, and then shook her head before either of them could answer. "No, I won't tell you. Ask your grandmother, Larissa."

They found Larissa's grandmother by the door, wrapped in her shawl. "It is recited at Amrit Sanchar," she said simply, "the Khalsa initiation ceremony. When you take amrit, Japji Sahib is part of it." Larissa went quiet, and Sydney let the information digest. The prayer her friend was memorizing wasn't just a morning habit. It would be spoken on one of the biggest days of her life, in front of everyone.

"Then we'd better not mess it up," Sydney said. She flipped the notebook back to the first page. "Ik Onkar. Again."

Larissa closed her eyes.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a string at its exact midpoint halves the length that vibrates, and the note rises by one octave.
story:
Bentley sat on the piano bench in Mr. Huang's studio, but the instrument in his lap was a guitar he had borrowed from his cousin, and it was winning. He had spent a week practicing the chord changes for the recital piece, and in the practice room at school the chords had sounded almost clean. Here, under Mr. Huang's ear, every chord buzzed like a parliament of angry magpies arguing over a crumb.

"You're pressing too hard," Mr. Huang said, which was strange, because in the practice room Bentley had been told he wasn't pressing hard enough.

"I don't get it," Bentley admitted. "Same guitar, same me. Why does it sound different here?"

Alycia, who was waiting for her lesson on the bench by the window, looked up from her phone. "Maybe your cousin's guitar is haunted."

"Very helpful."

She grinned, but Bentley kept turning it over. Something was different between the two rooms. He hadn't changed. His hands hadn't changed. The songs hadn't changed. In the practice room he sat in a low chair; here he perched on a tall piano bench, guitar sliding off his thigh. His left hand stretched at a steeper angle, reaching, and a stretched hand clamps instead of presses.

"Mr. Huang, can I try the chair?"

Mr. Huang raised an eyebrow, then waved him toward the folding chair by the door. Bentley sat, planted his feet, and played the same chord that had buzzed thirty seconds before. It rang clean, and he laughed out loud.

While Mr. Huang fetched the metronome, Bentley, feeling bold, plucked the open low string and let it hum. Then he pressed down at the twelfth fret, halfway along the neck, and plucked again. The sound was the same note, only higher. He tried it three more times, pressing at the exact middle of the string each time, and every time the open string's note came back, lifted. He could feel something invisible working, a rule hiding inside the wood and wire.

"Mr. Huang, why does the middle sound like the same note, just higher?"

"That's called an octave," Mr. Huang said. "Rest your finger directly over the twelfth fret and touch lightly, don't press."

Bentley tried it. The string whispered out a bell-like note, pure and floating, the octave again without his finger even pressing down. Alycia left her phone in her bag and came to stand beside him.

"I have to confide something," she said, low enough that only Bentley could hear. "I've been terrified of the recital for two weeks. I was going to fake being sick."

Bentley played the harmonic one more time. "Sit in the chair," he said. "It helps."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements that had not been discovered yet, and later discoveries such as gallium filled them.
story:
Jordan had meant to resent the whole assignment, and he told his grandfather so while carrying the box of old science books up from the basement. "Mr. Munro says we have to memorize the atomic numbers of twenty elements by Monday," he said, setting the box on the kitchen table. "Twenty. And half of them I can't even pronounce."

His grandfather, who was frail enough now that climbing the basement stairs took him a while, lowered himself into a chair and started flipping through the box. "Have a look at this one," he said, pulling out a thin paperback with a cracked spine. "I bought it secondhand when I was about your age. The landlord of the bookshop practically gave it away."

Jordan opened it and found a folded chart at the back, a periodic table printed in faded ink. Most of it looked familiar, rows of boxes with letters and numbers. Then he noticed something strange. Several boxes were empty. Just blanks with dashes where names should be, sitting in neat positions among the filled ones. "Why would anyone print a table with holes in it?" he asked. "Was it a misprint?"

"That's what I wondered too," his grandfather said, tapping the page but saying nothing more, which was his way of making Jordan work for things.

Jordan pulled out his phone and texted Angelica, who was the one person in his class who actually enjoyed this stuff. He wrote: old periodic table with blank boxes, why? While he waited, he tried something with the chart itself. He found carbon, saw the number 6 at the top of its box, and counted: six protons. He checked neon, atomic number 10, and thought ten protons, which felt obvious once he looked. Then oxygen, number 8. It worked every time, like a rule hiding under the numbers. The atomic number wasn't just a label. It told you something you couldn't see, something about particles way too small to look at, and the chart gave you a way to count them anyway.

Angelica texted back a long message, and Jordan read it out loud. "Mendeleev, the guy who built the first table, left gaps in it on purpose. He predicted elements nobody had found yet." Jordan ran his finger over the empty boxes again. So they weren't mistakes. They were guesses, waiting. He scrolled down in her message. "One of the gaps got filled by gallium when somebody finally discovered it. It fit right where the blank had been."

Jordan looked at his grandfather, then back at the chart, then grabbed a pencil. "Can I keep this book?" he asked. "I want to figure out which gap gallium filled."

His grandfather smiled and pushed the salt shaker aside to make room. "Start counting," he said.

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: On a river bend, water flows fastest on the outside, eroding that bank, and slowest on the inside, where it deposits sand and gravel.
story:
The science museum was hiring junior docents for the summer, and the interview was simple: stand at the big water table in the River Power exhibit and explain to visitors how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. Brooke had signed up because the job came with a name tag and free admission, but now she had a problem. Mr. Cardinal, who ran the program, had watched her rehearse with Shea and Shania and said her explanation sounded like she was reciting a card. "Learn the table first," he said. "Then talk."

The table was a long basin of pale sand with water pumped through it from one end to the other. You could shape the sand with your hands, and a crank let you change the speed of the current. Brooke bent the sand into a single curve, like a letter C lying down, and turned the crank to medium. Shea stood on her left, Shania on her right, both leaning over the glass.

"Watch the outside of the bend," Brooke said. She dropped a pinch of confetti near the top of the curve, and they all followed it. The pieces shot along the far bank, the outside wall of the curve, moving so fast they blurred. Confetti dropped near the inside bank crawled, barely drifting. "Fastest on the outside," Brooke said. "Slowest on the inside."

Within a few minutes the sand showed it. The outside bank, where the fast water hit, steepened into a cut wall, collapsing in small slices and washing downstream. The inside bank grew a smooth apron of pale sand and fine gravel that widened every time they looked. Shania pointed at it. "It's building a little beach." Brooke nodded. "That's deposition," she said. "The slow water drops what it's carrying, right there on the inside." Shea traced the deep channel hugging the outer wall with one finger above the glass, not quite touching.

Brooke tested it twice more. She made a tighter curve and the outside bank eroded faster; she made a gentler one and it eroded slower, but always on the outside, never the inside. The pattern held every time. She straightened up and looked at the whole table, the cut bank and the beach sitting opposite each other on the same bend, and thought about millions of years of this, the river swinging side to side, chewing down and laying down at once.

She turned the pump off and the water went opaque with stirred silt, so she waited for it to settle. Mr. Cardinal came back with a clipboard. "You have five minutes," he said. "Show me." Brooke pointed at the bend. "The water runs fastest on the outside of the bend, so it erodes that bank. On the inside it's slowest, so it drops its sand and gravel there. A river doing that over millions of years carves a canyon." Mr. Cardinal looked at the table, then at her. "Better," he said. "Now say it to a stranger." The first stranger through the door was a boy with a juice box, and Brooke stepped forward and asked, "Want to see a canyon get started?"

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: An "upstander" is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander.
story:
The birthday party was in Addison's backyard, which smelled like charcoal and sunscreen, and Levi was on his second slice of cake when Kenneth started in on a kid named Milo from their class. Milo had worn the same dinosaur backpack since fourth grade, and Kenneth thought this was hilarious in the way that only seventh graders can. "Nice backpack," Kenneth said, loud enough for the whole picnic table. "Does it commute to school with you, or does it walk?" A couple of kids laughed. Milo stared at his plate.

Levi knew the feeling. Two weeks ago, at lunch, some kids had gone after his friend's shoes, and Levi had sat there chewing, pretending to be deeply interested in his milk carton. The next day Ms. Villanueva's class had a discussion about it. She'd said one sentence and then moved on, and it had stuck in Levi's head like a burr: "An upstander is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander." Levi had spent the rest of the day wondering which word described what he'd done at lunch. Bystander, obviously. He'd been a bystander with a milk carton.

Here was the thing, though. He'd also learned, from a failed attempt on the bus, that yelling "Leave him alone, jerk" just gave everyone a better show. The teasing moved to him, then doubled back on the original kid, and the whole thing got worse. So there was a rule in there somewhere, invisible but real: attention was the fuel. If you made a big loud thing of it, you fed the fire. His idea was that the opposite might work. Don't attack. Don't lecture. Just quietly move the attention somewhere harmless.

He picked up the water balloon from beside his chair. "Milo," he said, "you still owe me a rematch from the arcade. I've been practicing." This was not exactly true, but it was true enough. Milo looked up, cautious, like a dog checking whether the stick was real. "You did not practice anything," Milo said. "I watched you lose to a claw machine on Saturday." The table's attention drifted toward the claw machine story, which involved Levi, a plastic penguin, and a certain amount of public humiliation that was safe because he was telling it himself. By the time he finished, Kenneth had wandered off toward the piñata, and nobody was looking at the backpack.

Later, Milo found him by the drinks. "That was decent of you," Milo said. "You didn't have to do the whole balloon thing." Levi shrugged. "I've been thinking about that word Ms. Villanueva said. Upstander. I figured there's probably a dumb way and a smart way to be one." Milo considered this, sipping his punch. "So which were you?" "The smart way," Levi said. "Obviously." Milo tipped his cup, and a single red drop landed on Levi's shoe.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, anon means at once or soon, so a servant calling "Anon!" is saying "Coming right away!"
story:
Ms. MacLeod handed out the copies of Romeo and Juliet, and Victoria slid hers to the corner of the desk where the shadow from the window wouldn't fall across the words. Jayden groaned beside her, but quietly, because Ms. MacLeod had already assigned parts. Victoria had the servant, a part with almost no words at all, which was why she'd wanted it. She still remembered last year, when she'd frozen during the class play and Alejandro had to whisper her whole line to her. She wasn't going to be the person who froze again, even if it meant taking the smallest role in the room.

Then she read her part and frowned. The servant had one word. Three times, whenever someone called from offstage, the servant shouted "Anon!" at the door. That was it. "Anon, anon!" Jayden read the calling lines in a big dramatic voice, and Victoria said "Anon!" and felt ridiculous, because she had no idea what she was saying.

She tried a hypothetical version in her head: what if "Anon" were the servant's name? It didn't fit. Nobody called him that. They called "Boy!" and "What, ho!" and he answered "Anon, anon!" every single time. Victoria tapped her pencil and looked at the pattern. Someone calls. He answers with the same word. Then he shows up. She remembered the French word "à présent," which her grandmother used on the phone, always meaning now, soon, on my way. What if "Anon" worked like that? She wrote "Coming right away!" in the margin, small, in pencil so she could erase it if she turned out to be wrong.

"Okay," Ms. MacLeod said, "paraphrase your speeches into modern English, in your groups. Victoria, you first, since your servant has the least to say."

Victoria took a breath. "When they call him, he says 'Anon,' and I think it means at once or soon. So a servant calling 'Anon!' is saying, coming right away." She gripped the desk, ready to be wrong.

Jayden flipped to the footnotes at the back of the book and ran his finger down the page. He couldn't refute her; the note said the same thing, right there in tiny print. "You got it," he said, and Alejandro held out his fist for her to bump.

"Read it again," Ms. MacLeod said. "With the meaning this time."

Jayden bellowed his line from across the room, and Victoria called "Anon! Coming right away!" at the door, loud enough that the class in the next room probably heard her.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Delayed muscle soreness is not caused by lactic acid, which returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise.
story:
Alice leaned on the chain-link fence behind first base, pressing her palm against her sore right shoulder. Nahla jogged over from the pitcher's mound and dropped her glove on the dirt beside her.

"It's the lactic acid," Nahla said. "My brother says that's what makes you sore after you pitch."

Alice frowned. "We pitched yesterday at practice. If lactic acid were the problem, it should have showed up right away, not today." She had read something about this in the sports medicine book Ms. Lin kept on the shelf in the equipment shed, and one detail stuck with her: lactic acid returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise. She turned that over in her head. "So your arms should have felt fine by the time we walked home yesterday. The soreness started this morning."

"So it's not lactic acid at all," Nahla said. "It's something else."

"It's something that happens later. A day later, maybe." Alice picked up her glove. "Which means it's not something you can fix by resting for an hour after pitching."

Avianna called from the dugout. "Are you two planning to play, or are you taking a science class out here?"

They took the field. Alice played second base, and by the fourth inning her legs were heavy with fatigue, though nothing hurt the way her shoulder had hurt that morning. When a ground ball skipped toward her, she kept her glove low, fielded it cleanly, and threw to first without trying to be aggressive about it. The runner was out by two steps.

Between innings she crouched beside Avianna near the water cooler. "Yesterday after practice I sat around for an hour and then biked home," Alice said. "If lactic acid caused the soreness, that rest should have cleared it, because it's back to normal within about an hour after exercise. But I woke up sore anyway. So sitting still after pitching doesn't help."

"Then what does help?" Avianna asked.

"Moving, maybe. Gently. Not sitting." Alice stood and swung her arms in slow circles. "Ms. Lin had us walk laps after the hard practice last week, remember? I wasn't sore the next morning."

Nahla jogged over from shortstop. "You're revising your whole warmup based on this?"

"I'm revising my whole cooldown," Alice said. "Walk it off tomorrow, don't just collapse on the couch."

In the seventh inning, with the tying run on third, Alice ranged to her left, backhanded a line drive that most players would never have reached, and fired to first to end the game. Her legs ached, but her shoulder felt loose. On the walk to the fence she turned to Nahla.

"Tell your brother he's wrong about the lactic acid," she said. "And tell him he owes me a slushie."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Open-ended questions, which cannot be answered with just yes or no, usually get longer answers and keep a conversation going.
story:
Lincoln had the phone in his hand for twenty minutes before he texted Blair. "It died," he typed. "The whole thing. Like a minute in." He and Maina had gone to the coffee shop after school, and it had started fine, and then he had asked if she liked Mr. Pemberton's class, and she said no, and he asked if she liked the school play, and she said yes, and then they both drank their hot chocolates until the cups were empty. He had walked her home anyway, and she had said "see you," which could mean anything.

"You asked yes-or-no questions the whole time," Blair texted back. "Everyone does that when they're nervous. It's like a quiz."

Lincoln stared at the message. He scrolled back through the afternoon in his head, counting. Do you like school. Do you have brothers. Is the hot chocolate good. Blair was right. Every question he'd asked could be answered in one word, and every one had been. It was like there was a hidden rule running the whole conversation, and he'd been following it without knowing it existed. Maybe, he thought, if a question couldn't be answered with yes or no, it couldn't be answered in one word either. It was worth testing. Maina had said see you, so he texted her, apologized for being weird, and asked if she wanted to try again Saturday.

She said yes.

Saturday, at the same table by the window, Lincoln was ready. When the drinks came, instead of asking if hers was good, he asked what she would order if the coffee shop had no menu and she had to invent a drink. Maina put down her cup. "Okay, so. It would have to have caramel," she said, "but also something weird, like black pepper, because my grandma puts pepper on strawberries and everyone thinks she's insane but it's actually amazing." That led to her grandma, which led to the summer Maina's family had boycotted the whole grocery store over a fight about a dented can, which led to her dad standing in the parking lot holding a hand-lettered sign. She talked so long Lincoln's hot chocolate went cold, and he barely noticed.

He kept it going all afternoon. What was the most gullible thing she'd ever believed, he asked, and she confessed she had believed in the tooth fairy until fifth grade because her mom kept leaving extremely detailed notes in tiny handwriting. He asked what she would do if she could skip one year of school entirely, and she said seventh, without hesitating, and then went quiet and told him why, and he listened. An hour and a half went by like ten minutes. When they finally left, she held the door for him and said, "You're way easier to talk to than you were last time."

He was still glowing about it on Monday until Blair cornered him by the lockers, grinning. "So how'd your experiment go, scientist?"

"Perfect," Lincoln said. "She did almost all the talking."

Blair clapped him on the shoulder. "Then she asked me Thursday night what your favorite song is. Said she didn't want another silent car ride. Guess you'd better come up with an answer."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A thesis can preview the argument by naming its supporting points in the same order the body paragraphs will discuss them.
story:
Lauren spread her essay drafts across the corner table of the Sunhill Cafe, three napkins weighing down the curling pages. The topic stared back at her: Should the voting age be lowered to sixteen? Her teacher wanted a thesis statement and an outline with three supporting points before anyone wrote a full draft, and Lauren had a draft anyway, which was the problem.

"You're doing it backwards," said Edith, sliding into the seat across from her with a hot chocolate. "Ms. Owusu said thesis first."

"Ms. Owusu doesn't have to read my handwriting," Lauren said, but she pulled out a fresh sheet of paper. She had written three body paragraphs last night. One argued that sixteen-year-olds pay taxes on their part-time jobs, so they should have a say. One argued that they can already drive, which is more dangerous than voting. One argued that other countries let them vote at sixteen, so it clearly works.

She wrote her thesis at the top of the page: Sixteen-year-olds should get the vote because they pay taxes, they can already drive, and other countries have proved it works. Then she numbered her points one, two, three to match. Perfect. She leaned back and drank her lukewarm tea.

Dereck arrived twenty minutes late, shaking rain off his jacket, and read over her shoulder while he waited for his muffin. "Your driving paragraph is way stronger than the taxes one," he said. "Start with it. My brother says always open with your best punch."

Lauren reread the paragraphs. He was right about which was stronger. She picked up her pen, drew arrows, and reordered the outline: driving first, taxes second, other countries third. Then she looked back up at her thesis and stopped. "Wait," she said. "My thesis says taxes, driving, other countries. But my outline now goes driving, taxes, other countries."

Edith frowned at the page. "So the reader hits the driving paragraph first, but the thesis promised taxes first?"

"Right." Lauren read the thesis again, mouthing it. It wasn't wrong exactly, but it was like a table of contents that listed the chapters out of order. She crossed out the old version and wrote a new one, moving the words around the same way she had moved the paragraphs: Sixteen-year-olds should get the vote because they can already drive, they pay taxes on their jobs, and other countries have proved it works. The order in the sentence now matched the order in the outline, point for point.

The cafe owner, who was planning to retire at the end of the year and had told every regular customer about it at least twice, brought Dereck his muffin and glanced at the paper. "Homework about the parliament? You kids are ambitious."

"It's about voting," Lauren said. She copied the reordered thesis onto a clean card so it wouldn't get lost under the napkins. Monday she would hand in the outline, and for once the whole thing would line up.

"Read it to me one more time," Edith said.

Lauren held up the card. "Sixteen-year-olds should get the vote because they can already drive, they pay taxes on their jobs, and other countries have proved it works."

"Conventional," Dereck said, mouth full of muffin, "but solid."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: The volt, the unit of voltage, is named after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta.
story:
Beatrice sat on the low concrete ledge at the edge of the skate park with a battery, a thin coil of wire, a voltmeter, and a multimeter borrowed from her uncle's toolbox. Her homework was due Monday: measure the voltage across a wire, measure the current through it, and calculate the resistance. The trouble was that her numbers kept coming out wrong, and she could not see why, because resistance was not something you could watch like a skater wiping out on the half-pipe.

"You look like you're doing surgery on a sandwich," said Romy, rolling to a stop beside her, wheels grinding grit across the pavement. Zainab coasted up on the other side, eating a popsicle that dripped orange down her wrist.

"I'm trying to diagnose my circuit," Beatrice said. "Something's hiding in there. Every time I run it, the resistance answer changes, so something I'm not controlling must be a variable." She frowned at the coil. Last night the wire had sat dormant in her backpack, cold and untouched, and this morning it had warmed in the sun on the ledge. She laid her palm against it. Warm. She wondered whether heat could be the hidden cause, the thing she could not see directly.

She ran the test again, holding the wire up out of the sun so it stayed cool, and this time the numbers held steady. Voltage divided by current gave the same resistance twice in a row. "Ha!" she said, and did a small seated victory bounce that nearly knocked the multimeter off the ledge.

"Okay, explain like I'm a popsicle," Zainab said.

"Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance is what the wire pushes back with," Beatrice said, packing up. "The meter measures voltage in volts. Guess who that's named after? Alessandro Volta. An Italian physicist. My uncle told me at the science museum last summer, there was a whole battery exhibit with his name on it."

Romy squinted. "So if I get shocked on the rail over there, is that a volta?"

"That's just static, and also please don't." Beatrice clipped the leads together and stood, slinging her backpack over one shoulder. She looked at the long metal rail gleaming in the afternoon light, then at the battery in her hand. "Tomorrow I test the same wire cold and hot, three runs each, and graph it."

"Science at a skate park," Zainab said, dropping her stick in the trash. "Mr. Dang would faint."

From across the bowl, Mr. Dang, who coached the Tuesday beginners group, cupped his hands and called, "Homework on my ledge means you owe me a lap!"

Beatrice laughed and picked up her board. "Fine, but I'm timing it, and don't blame me if the slope is the variable."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture.
story:
The heritage wall went up on Friday, and every student had to hand in a card with three words describing where they were from. Zachary had written his in two minutes: Portland, Oregon, the whole time. The new kid, Monroe, sat with a blank card in front of him for most of Thursday's class, tapping his pencil like it might start writing on its own.

"You lived in Brazil, right?" Zachary said at lunch. "Just put Brazil."

"I lived there for two years. Also Singapore, Germany, and Egypt. Four countries." Monroe tore the crust off his sandwich. "Everybody keeps asking where I'm from, and when I start listing places, their eyes kind of glaze over."

Frederick leaned across the table. "Pick the one you liked best. That's your answer."

But Monroe said the question felt like a shirt that restricted him, like it only came in one size and he didn't fit it. Zachary thought about that all through afternoon classes. There had to be a name for people like Monroe. Kids who moved like that couldn't be the first ones ever. Somebody, somewhere, must have noticed the pattern and called it something. After the last bell, he asked Ms. Andersen if he could use the library computers before it closed, and she said he had twenty minutes because the building locked at four.

He typed in words like "kid who lived in many countries." That gave him travel blogs. He tried "growing up abroad." That was closer. One result mentioned a sociologist, an American named Ruth Hill Useem, who had coined a term back in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture. Zachary read the phrase twice. Third culture kid. It sounded strange and right at the same time, like a name for a thing you'd seen your whole life without knowing it had one. He copied it onto his hand with a pen, because his notebook was in his locker and the librarian was already jingling her keys.

Friday morning, Zachary found Monroe at the blank wall outside Ms. Andersen's room, card still empty, deadline ten minutes away. "Try this," Zachary said. "Third culture kid."

Monroe stared at him. "Say it again."

"Third culture kid. It's a real thing. A sociologist came up with it."

Monroe wrote it down, then added three more words underneath: adaptable, tired, lucky. He pinned the card between Frederick's Ireland card and a girl's card about her grandmother's village in Kerala. Ms. Andersen walked by, read Monroe's card, and nodded once, the way she did when something was exactly right.

At recess Monroe was telling three kids from second period about his school in Singapore, how the lunch breaks were longer and how everyone swapped languages in the middle of sentences. He had more stamina for the story than Zachary expected, like the question had been holding all of it in. When the bell rang, Monroe turned around, walking backward toward the door.

"You know what the weird part is?" he called. "I didn't know there was a word for me either."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept up high and out of reach, because young children explore by putting things in their mouths.
story:
Nicolas pressed the doorbell of number fourteen with his thumb, then wiped his palm on his jeans. Ms. Rodríguez opened the door with a toddler on her hip and a folder of papers under her arm. "You must be Nicolas. The emergency numbers are on the fridge, and my sister's coming by nine." She set the little girl, Pia, down on the carpet, handed him a bag of crackers, and hurried off to a late meeting at the school where she taught.

For the first ten minutes, babysitting was exactly what Nicolas had imagined. Pia stacked blocks, knocked them over, and laughed like each crash was a brand-new invention. Nicolas stacked a tower of his own to see if she would copy it, and she did, which made him feel like a genius scientist. Then he got up to refill her sippy cup, and when he came back from the kitchen, the living room had gone quiet in a way that made the hair on his arms stand up.

Pia was on her hands and knees near the coffee table, reaching for something. Nicolas crossed the room in three steps and saw a bottle of orange vitamins sitting right at the edge, low enough for her small fingers to brush the cap. He remembered his mother saying the words once at their own house, medicines and cleaning products up high, out of reach, because little kids explore by putting things in their mouths. Pia, meanwhile, had already proven the point: she was chewing on the remote control with great focus.

He lifted the bottle to the highest shelf of the bookcase, then checked the room like a detective. Under the bathroom sink he found a spray bottle of cleaner behind a stack of towels, low and easy to grab, and he carried that up high too. To keep himself honest, he took out his phone and photographed each spot before and after, planning to document everything so Ms. Rodríguez could see exactly what he had moved and why. Pia supervised from the doorway, cracker in each fist, shouting a word that might have been "up."

The sister arrived at nine, but Ms. Rodríguez came home ten minutes later, tired and carrying a paper bag of leftovers. "How was she?" she asked, and Nicolas showed her the photos. She scrolled through them slowly, and her tired face changed. "The vitamins were on the coffee table? I could have sworn I put them away." She looked at the high shelf, then at Pia, who was attempting to eat the remote again. "You just earned yourself a regular job, Nicolas. A distinct improvement over my last sitter, who spent the whole evening on his phone." Nicolas grinned. "Actually, I was on mine. But only for evidence." Ms. Rodríguez laughed and held up the bottle of vitamins. "Next time," she said, "I'll put these so high even I can't reach them."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
Kenza wanted an answer by nine o'clock, because at nine she was going to post a photo of her new house, street sign and all, so her cousins could find her after the move. "Just tell me if it's a bad idea," her message said. Lea typed back that she'd check something first, though she wasn't sure what.

An hour earlier, Trace had sent her a link with the words "you won't believe this." It led to a blog Lea had written in fourth grade, the one she'd deleted two years ago, complete with a photo of her in front of her old school and a post that said exactly which park she went to every Saturday. "How is it still there?" she had asked Trace. Trace said he didn't know, but that his brother had found some site that keeps old pages. "It's called the Wayback Machine," Trace wrote. "You just put in an address."

Lea pulled up the site. In the search box she typed her old blog's address, half expecting an error. Instead a calendar appeared, dotted with dates. She clicked one from three years ago, and there was her nine-year-old self, announcing to the entire internet which bench she sat on and when. Anyone, anywhere, could be reading it, and had been able to for years without her knowing. She felt her face go hot. Deleting had seemed so final at the time.

She thought about Kenza's photo. The street sign wouldn't just reach the cousins; it would sit there, waiting, the way Lea's park post had waited. Maybe it would even get copied into an archive, though she didn't understand how that worked. She decided to test it the only way she could: she opened the archive again and searched a few other pages she remembered, including a site Trace had made and abandoned. The Wayback Machine had that too. Whatever this thing was, it had been quietly saving copies of public web pages since 1996, and it wasn't picky.

At 8:41 Lea called Kenza. "Don't post the street sign," she said. "Send your cousins the picture in a message instead. It turns out stuff doesn't really go away. I found my old blog, the one I deleted, still readable." There was a pause on the line.

"Still readable? Like, strangers could see it?"

"Anyone. That's how I found it." Lea heard Kenza breathing, thinking.

"Okay," Kenza said slowly. "New plan. No sign, just the house. And Lea? See if you can find my old swim team page in that machine. I want to know what's out there."

Lea grinned, cracked her knuckles, and started typing.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: A split is the time for one section of a race; an 800-metre runner's 400-metre split shows right away whether the first lap was faster or slower than planned.
story:
The cones were still wet from morning rain when Matthew lined up on the far curve of the soccer field, which Mr. Owusu had measured into a rough four-hundred-metre loop. He had one job today, and it was not to run fast. "First lap, steady," Billie called from the sideline, clipboard in hand. "Remember what happened last time." Matthew remembered it well: he had charged out like the finish line was two hundred metres away, and by the second lap his legs had turned to rope.

At the whistle he went out hard anyway. It felt controlled, it felt easy, and that was the trap. When he thundered past the start line at the end of lap one, Mr. Owuso's voice cut across the field. "Fifty-eight seconds!" Matthew's stomach dropped. He had planned sixty-six. Billie sprinted alongside him for a few strides, holding up the watch. "That's your split, Matt. Fifty-eight. Way faster than you meant to go."

He tried to fix it on the spot. Instead of surging, he shortened his stride and counted his breaths, four steps in, four steps out, testing whether the count could hold him together. His arms burned, but the count held. Behind him he heard Samir yelling, "You're not dying, you're just scared you're dying, which is different!" That made him laugh, which cost him a breath, which somehow helped.

He crossed the line in two minutes and eleven seconds, and then he bent over with his hands on his knees while the drizzle began to saturate his shoulders. Billie read the clipboard. "So the split tells you right away. Fifty-eight means the first lap was faster than planned. If it had come up slow, that's the other problem." Matthew nodded, still gasping. Fifty-eight. Faster. He could see now that the first lap had lied to him, that feeling easy at the start was not the same thing as being on pace.

They ran it twice more. On the third try he counted from the very first stride, and when Mr. Owusu shouted "Sixty-five!" at the line, Matthew felt something loosen in his chest, because sixty-five was almost exactly the number he had chosen. The second lap still hurt, a vigorous, full-body hurt, but it was a hurt with room left in it. He finished strong enough to pass Samir, who was jogging the loop just to keep him company. Afterward Mr. Owusu clapped him on the back and said the van was leaving in ten minutes, and Matthew had an obligation to help load the cones. He picked up the nearest one, tucked it under his arm, and grinned at Billie. "Same time Thursday?"
